intro: How does Clark County's spending compare to its neighbors — and which categories deserve a closer look? Comparisons here are per resident, from each county's own filed 2026 budget. They are ballpark by nature: Arkansas counties structure funds differently (Ouachita runs its sheriff out of a jail fund; Garland has a dedicated detention sales tax), so treat these as the start of questions, not the end of them.

headline_rows.label: General Fund (courthouse government, law enforcement, courts)
headline_rows.note: Clark spends more per resident than Garland — the small-county scale penalty: one sheriff, one clerk's office, one courthouse divide across five times fewer people. Ouachita's general fund total is not yet summed from its department-level filing.

headline_rows.label: Sheriff's office
headline_rows.note: Nearly identical spend rates per resident — yet Garland pays deputies about $14,000 more. Same dollars, less salary: scale again. Ouachita's sheriff budget sits inside its Jail Operating fund and is not line-comparable.

twin_note: Ouachita County (~22,000 people, Camden) is Clark's closest size twin. Most office budgets land in the same ballpark — evidence that Clark's administrative structure is normal for its size, not bloated. The one line running well above the twin: courthouse maintenance, flagged below.

outliers.title: EDCCC incentives — $1.84M/yr
outliers.body: $88 per resident per year — four times the library, forty times the health department — appropriated as a single word with no public recipient list. $25.4M collected from 2008 through 2023 (audited).

outliers.title: The hospital and college mills — ~$700K/yr not in the county appropriation ordinance
outliers.body: The state millage book shows 1 mill each levied county-wide for the hospital and the college. At the county's ~$346M assessed value (derived from the FY2023 audit's debt-limit figure), that is roughly $346,000 a year each — flowing to those institutions without ever appearing in the county's appropriation ordinance. Possibly entirely proper; documented nowhere we can navigate.

outliers.title: The library spends about a third of what it collects
outliers.body: ~$1.28M projected revenue, $469K appropriated, ~$883K sitting unappropriated (including a $196K bequest). A building fund? A policy? No document in the corpus says.

outliers.title: The 911 reserve holds $1.01M idle
outliers.body: While dispatcher staffing and pay are live issues in the same system, the reserve fund appropriates $118K of a $1.26M balance.

outliers.title: The road-bond sales tax: receipts about match the payments
outliers.body: A 0.5% sales tax pledge repays the $8.46M Truck Bypass bonds (2021, 1.125–2.00%, through 2036). We earlier guessed it might raise far more than the debt costs; the audits say otherwise. The bond fund took in $469,373 in 2022 and $678,806 in 2023, against debt payments of $341,005 and $670,756. Any excess may be used for any lawful purpose. The bond ordinance itself is not yet in this corpus.

outliers.title: About $1M/yr of vague pool lines
outliers.body: Road "other professional services" ($350K), jail "contracts" ($351K), sanitation engineering and professional services ($325K) — single lines, no stated recipients. Check-register territory.

outliers.title: Courthouse maintenance runs ~$162K above the twin county
outliers.body: $416K vs Ouachita's $254K. The gap sits mostly in a $100K property-maintenance pool and $66.5K of insurance — explainable, but unexplained.

summary: The arithmetic: roads, public safety, and sanitation — direct service — are about two-thirds of everything the county spends. In the remaining third, the documentation thins out: roughly $4M a year moves without public detail (EDCCC, the hospital and college mills, pooled lines, fee funds), and roughly $4M more sits unappropriated — some of that required by the state's 90% rule. This page draws no conclusion about any of it. Every item above is a trail that stops short of a receipt, a document that would extend it, and a docket number tracking the ask.
